time.interpretation: 1122–1133 dates the composition of the surviving textual account. It is not a monk-arrival interval, an occupation duration, a date of surviving manuscript material or an eleven-year voyage.

claims.text: Ari’s early-twelfth-century Íslendingabók describes Irish Christian residents called papar before Norse settlement in Iceland.
claims.explanation: Chapter 1 reports their departure and interprets objects they allegedly left as Irish. The introductory dating comes from the bishops addressed in Ari’s prologue.

support.locator: Introduction p.xiii; chapter 1 p.4
support.note: Composition 1122–1133 and the account of earlier Irish Christian residents.

claims.text: Ari’s account does not securely establish when or where Irish monks lived in Iceland.
claims.explanation: The story is later testimony. The checked scholarly assessments do not identify securely attributable pre-Norse monastic archaeology; readings of Dicuil and place names remain debated.

support.locator: Note 18, p.17
support.note: Discusses Irish monastic voyaging, possible place-name transmission and absence of archaeological corroboration.

support.locator: Discussion of Ari, Dicuil, Papey and archaeological remains
support.note: Explains why the sources do not prove a specific Icelandic monastic settlement.

sources.authors: Ari Þorgilsson; translated with introduction and notes by Siân Grønlie
sources.title: Íslendingabók — Kristni saga: The Book of the Icelanders — The Story of the Conversion
sources.venue: Viking Society for Northern Research, Text Series XVIII
sources.access: Publisher PDF downloaded and read: introduction p.xiii, chapter 1 p.4, and note 18 p.17. Chapter page visually checked. Source composition is dated 1122–1133, not 2006.
sources.publisher: Viking Society for Northern Research, University College London

sources.authors: Axel Kristinsson; translated by Nicholas Jones
sources.title: Is there any tangible proof that there were Irish monks in Iceland before the time of the Viking settlements?
sources.venue: University of Iceland, Icelandic Web of Science
sources.access: Full scholarly answer read; evaluates Ari, Dicuil, place names and archaeological ambiguity. This dated assessment is not represented as a new archaeological survey.

review.summary: A recorded tradition about possible Irish Christian predecessors, presented at the date of the text that attests it.
review.limitations: The reference coordinate is only for Iceland as the subject of the narrative. It is not Ari’s writing desk, Papey monastery, a landing point, or a sailing destination. No precise arrival year or route is assigned.
review.discussion: Papar is normally interpreted here as Irish monks or religious exiles. Their possible presence remains distinguishable from Ari’s securely observable statement. Dicuil’s Thule and Brendan traditions are not promoted into verified tracks.
review.provenance: Norse continuity and settlement-end source audit; regional occupation, dated events and later literary testimony kept distinct.
